extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate (or advanced high-school) students and general readers studying introductory calculus and minimal-surface phenomena
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from an introductory textbook chapter that explains physical experiments on minimal surfaces (soap films) and introduces the integral as the limit of Riemann sums, with historical and geometric context. It presents definitions, examples, and guiding remarks for understanding and computing integrals and for interpreting soap-film minimal-surface phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean curvature definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean curvature of a surface at a point P is defined by considering the perpendicular to the surface at P and all planes containing it; these planes intersect the surface in curves with different curvatures at P. Take the curves of minimum and maximum curvature respectively; one-half the sum of these two curvatures is the mean curvature of the surface at P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains a geometric construction: consider principal normal sections (planes through normal), identify principal curvatures (min and max) and average them. (Text notes that the planes containing these principal-curvature curves will, in general, be perpendicular to each other.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Soap film realizes least-area (Plateau's) solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a closed wire contour is dipped into a low-surface-tension liquid and withdrawn, a film in the form of a minimal surface of least area will span the contour (assuming gravity and other interfering forces may be neglected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plateau's experiments provide physical solutions for very general contours; existence for general mathematical problem was proved by J. Douglas and T. Rado. The soap-film experiment is a practical method for 'solving' Plateau's problem by shaping the wire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical soap-solution and frame advice
rubrics_metrics.description: A recommended soap solution: dissolve 10 grams of pure dry sodium oleate in 500 grams of distilled water, and mix 15 cubic units of the solution with 11 cubic units of glycerin. Use brass-wire frames not exceeding five or six inches in diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Films obtained with this solution and with frames of brass wire are relatively stable; frames larger than recommended may be less stable. This is a practical experimental recipe for producing stable soap films for demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 120-degree intersection rule for soap films
rubrics_metrics.description: Surfaces produced by soap films often meet each other at angles of 120° along lines of intersection (for example, three surfaces meeting along a line intersect each at 120°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phenomenon appears repeatedly (e.g., three sheets meeting at 120°) and is related to generalizations of Steiner's problem and to the geometry of minimal-surface junctions; experiments preserve these 120° angles even as configurations deform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary contact orthogonality
rubrics_metrics.description: If parts of the boundary of a film are left free to move on given surfaces (such as planes), then on these boundaries the film will be perpendicular to the prescribed surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this property to create demonstrations of Steiner-type variational problems: films constrained to meet bounding surfaces will meet them at right angles (useful for projecting solutions onto plates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of solutions and stability (absolute vs relative minima)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the same prescribed contour there can be multiple minimal-surface solutions (different topologies or shapes); some are absolute minima of area while others are relative minima (stable locally). The stability of a solution can change as the boundary is deformed, and discontinuous transitions between solutions can occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a contour deformed can yield either a disk or a Möbius strip solution; for symmetric contours multiple simply connected solutions may have equal area; when symmetry is broken one becomes the absolute minimum and the other a local minimum. When the area differences are large, the less-area solution dominates and the other may be too unstable to form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catenoid instability and discontinuous transition
rubrics_metrics.description: A minimal surface of revolution (the catenoid) spanning two circles becomes unstable when the circles are pulled apart sufficiently; at that moment the catenoid jumps discontinuously into two separated disks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This transition is not reversible by the same continuous parameter change; experiments illustrate loss of stability and discontinuous changes in the minimizing configuration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surfaces of constant mean curvature for constrained bubbles
rubrics_metrics.description: When a soap bubble is constrained (for example, by bounding plates) and has a fixed enclosed volume, the equilibrium surface is a surface of constant mean curvature; spheres and circular cylinders are special examples. Among all closed surfaces enclosing a given volume, the sphere has the least area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a bubble between two parallel plates will assume a hemisphere when touching one plate and jump to a circular cylinder when touching both; by varying volume one can study isoperimetric behavior. These illustrate that constrained minimization leads to constant-mean-curvature solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral as limit of Riemann sums (area under a curve)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a function y = f(x) on [a,b], the area A under the curve (and above the x-axis) from a to b is defined as the limit of sums S_n = Σ f(x_i) Δx as the width of the largest subinterval tends to zero; this limiting value A is the integral ∫_a^b f(x) dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: subdivide [a,b] into n subintervals, pick a sample point in each subinterval, form rectangles of height f(sample) and width Δx, sum their areas, and take the limit as the mesh goes to zero. The limit is independent of the particular choice of sample points or subdivisions provided the mesh tends to zero. Historical Leibniz notation (Σ → ∫, Δ → d) is heuristic; modern definition rests on the limit concept, not infinitesimals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic-area convention for signed integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: When f(x) takes negative values on parts of [a,b], the integral ∫_a^b f(x) dx is the algebraic sum of areas bounded by the graph and the x-axis: areas below the x-axis are counted as negative and those above as positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows computing integrals without assuming f(x)≥0. Also, if the limits are reversed, ∫_a^b f(x) dx = −∫_b^a f(x) dx.

rubrics_metrics.name: General (Riemann) definition allowing unequal subintervals
rubrics_metrics.description: The integral may be defined using partitions with unequal subinterval widths: form sums Σ f(ξ_i) Δx_i where ξ_i is any point in [x_i, x_{i+1}]; the integral exists as the limit of these sums as the largest Δx_i tends to zero (mesh → 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The only restriction is that the norm (the largest subinterval length) tends to zero; under this condition different choices of points ξ_i and different partitions yield the same limit when the integral exists. A later (supplement) discussion promises a full existence proof for continuous functions without prior geometric area notion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/exhaustion approach to area (Archimedes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of a plane figure bounded by curves can be obtained by inscribing polygonal approximations and taking limits (method of exhaustion), as used by Archimedes for circles and parabolic segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides geometric motivation for the integral. The text contrasts the ancient 'exhaustion' approach (area assumed intuitively given) with the later rigorous limit-based approach of the calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic integral evaluation examples (power functions, constants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary integrals: (a) If f(x) is constant c, then ∫_a^b c dx = c(b−a). (b) For power functions x^k the integral over [a,b] yields (b^{k+1} − a^{k+1})/(k+1) (with discussion of the limiting derivation for rational k etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter gives worked limiting-sum derivations for these examples (including using geometric interpretations for ∫ x dx as trapezoid area) and exercises for various k (including negative and fractional). These are model computations showing the Riemann-sum method yields the expected formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic/reduction rules for integration (calculus procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The calculus provides general rules and procedures that reduce more involved integration problems to simpler ones, enabling mechanical/algorithmic solution of many integrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leibniz notation emphasizes the algorithmic feature, but the text warns against overemphasis on mechanical manipulation at the expense of conceptual understanding; the rules will be presented in following sections (§5 and onward).
